status: DRAFT v0.1: not yet reviewed, pretested or calibrated.
notes: High pole is consistently 'more room for religion in public institutions'.

items.stem: Which comes closer to your view of religion and government?
items.scope: Think about government at every level.

sides.label: Strict separation
sides.text: Keep them strictly separate, even if public life has less room for religious expression.

sides.label: Room for religion
sides.text: Let government support and reflect religion, even if people of other faiths or none feel left out.

items.stem: Which comes closer to your view of how lawmakers should decide?

sides.label: Shared reasons only
sides.text: Laws should rest on reasons everyone can share, not on religious teaching, even for lawmakers of deep faith.

sides.label: Faith can guide law
sides.text: Lawmakers should be free to base laws on their religious beliefs, even if others don't share them.

items.subtopic: Prayer and religious displays in public schools and buildings
items.stem: Should public schools lead students in prayer?
items.scope: Prayer organized by the school, not students praying on their own, which is always allowed.
options: No; schools should not sponsor prayer in any form
A moment of silence, but no led prayer
Teacher-led prayer that students can choose to skip
Daily prayer led by the school

items.subtopic: Prayer and religious displays in public schools and buildings
items.stem: Should the Ten Commandments be displayed in public school classrooms?
items.context: Several states have recently passed laws requiring this; courts are divided on them.
options: Only as part of a display on the history of law, alongside other documents

facts.claim: Louisiana (2024), Arkansas and Texas (2025) passed classroom display laws; federal courts have blocked some
facts.source: State statutes; Roake v. Brumley (5th Cir.)

items.stem: If public money can pay private school tuition, should families be able to use it at religious schools?
items.scope: Answer even if you oppose public money for private schools.
options: No; only at non-religious private schools
Yes, if religious classes are optional for those students
Yes, on equal terms with any other school

items.stem: Should a religious group be allowed to run a publicly funded, tuition-free charter school that teaches its faith?
items.scope: Charter schools are public schools run independently of the school district.
options: Yes, if students can opt out of religious instruction
Yes, like any other charter school

items.stem: When a law that applies to everyone conflicts with someone's religious beliefs, should they get an exemption?
items.scope: Think of laws in general. Specific cases come next.
options: Rarely; everyone should follow the same laws
Only when the exemption doesn't harm anyone else
Yes, in most cases, unless the government has a very strong reason

items.stem: Should each of these get a religious exemption?

cases.text: An employer that doesn't want its health plan to cover birth control
A church that uses a banned drug in its ceremonies
Parents who refuse medical treatment for their seriously ill child

items.stem: Should the US government officially declare the US a Christian nation?
items.scope: An official declaration by law, not a description of history.
options: No; government should favor no religion
No declaration, but government can recognize the nation's Christian heritage

items.stem: How important is it for the country that most Americans are religious?
items.scope: Any religion. This is about the country, not you personally.
options: Essential; the country's success depends on it
